7.0.s.en: 1. The inquiry of the people of Bethel:

7.0.0.en: 1 And it came to pass in the fourth year of king Darius, that the word of the LORD came unto Zechariah in the fourth day of the ninth month, even in Chisleu; 2 when the people of Bethel sent Sherezer and Regemmelech, and their men, to pray before the LORD, 3 and to speak unto the priests which were in the house of the LORD of hosts, and to the prophets, saying, Should I weep in the fifth month, separating myself, as I have done these so many years?

7.0.1.en: In the fourth year of Darius the king, that is, in 518 B.C., the people were working with great zeal in rebuilding the temple and the fruit of this work had appeared clearly, as the signs of ruin began to disappear from Jerusalem, so the people of Bethel sent two delegates, Sherezer and Regemmelech, and their men, to consult the priests who were in the house of the Lord and the prophets whether, after the appearance of this new life, there was still need to practice fasting and weeping in the fifth month (the tenth day) in remembrance of the burning of the house of the Lord (Jer 52:12-13; 2 Kgs 25:8-10), or whether they should stop it. This question carried two painful pictures: that fasting represented a burden in their lives which they wished to be rid of, and that it was an end in itself and was not practiced in the spirit of inner repentance and true change. Therefore the answer came carrying a rebuke on the one hand and a revelation of the concept of true spiritual fasting on the other.

7.1.0.en: 4 Then came the word of the LORD of hosts unto me, saying, 5 Speak unto all the people of the land, and to the priests, saying, When ye fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh month, even those seventy years, was it a fast unto me, even to me? 6 And when ye did eat, and when ye did drink, were ye not the eaters and ye the drinkers? 7 Is not this the word which the LORD hath cried by the former prophets, when Jerusalem was inhabited and at rest, and the cities thereof round about her, and the south and the plain inhabited?

7.2.0.en: Since the question carried a sign of distress and complaint on their part because of the fasting, and also carried a kind of hypocrisy, the Lord answered them that He has no need of their fasts; they fixed this fast by their own choice and it is their right to stop it without asking, but it befitted them in their fasting to practice it in a sincere spirit, and if they stopped it to rejoice in God's work with them... In other words, whether they fasted or ate, they did not offer offerings of love to God but mere outward practices. This is what He meant by His rebuke of them: “When ye fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh month, even those seventy years, was it a fast unto me, even to me? And when ye did eat, and when ye did drink, were ye not the eaters and ye the drinkers?” [5-6].

7.2.1.en: They asked about the fast of the fifth month, and He answered them also about the fast of the seventh month, which they established in remembrance of the killing of Gedaliah, governor of Judah, a matter that led to the scattering of the remnant of the Jews after the captivity (Jer 41:1-3), and He confirmed that they fasted these two fasts and others such as the fast of the tenth month in remembrance of the first siege of Jerusalem with catapults and the fast of the fourth month in remembrance of the capture of the city in the reign of Zedekiah (Jer 39:2; 52:6-7), as though He says to them, I know your fasts throughout this period, but I do not ask for the multitude of fasts but for their quality. You practiced them without returning to the Lord and not in obedience to the commandments but merely to calm their consciences.

7.2.2.en: In their minds fasting was merely abstaining from food and not from evil, and enjoying righteousness, therefore St. Didymus the Blind says: [We must restrain the stomach with the bonds of prostrations (metanoia) with tears! But how destructive it is for a man that his fast be like those who refuse to enjoy the bread of life (Jn 6:35), that is, the enjoyment of the Body of Jesus, the true Bread that came down from heaven?!]. St. Didymus again distinguishes between two kinds of fasting, offering the testimony of Holy Scripture, saying: [Concerning good fasting it is said in Joel: “Sanctify ye a fast, call a solemn assembly” (Joel 1:14; 2:15). And in another place He declares: “Prayer is good with fasting and alms, for it delivers from death” (Tob 12:8-9). As for the bad fast, we find the wicked and unbelievers accusing the Lord, saying: “Wherefore have we fasted, say they, and thou seest not? wherefore have we afflicted our soul, and thou takest no knowledge?” (Isa 58:3); and the Lord answers them saying: “Is it such a fast that I have chosen?” (Isa 58:5). So whoever avoids bad food must multiply good works. Truly the Scripture says: “To deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house; when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him, and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh; then shall thy light break forth as the morning, and thine health shall spring forth speedily” (Isa 58:7-8)].

7.3.0.en: 8 And the word of the LORD came unto Zechariah, saying, 9 Thus speaketh the LORD of hosts, saying, Execute true judgment, and do kindness and mercy, every man with his brother: 10 and oppress not the widow, nor the fatherless, nor the stranger, nor the poor; and let none of you imagine evil against his brother in your heart. 11 But they refused to hearken, and gave a stubborn shoulder, and made heavy their ears, that they should not hear. 12 Yea, they made their heart an adamant stone, lest they should hear the law, and the words which the LORD of hosts hath sent in his spirit by the former prophets: therefore came a great wrath from the LORD of hosts. 13 And it came to pass that as he cried, and they would not hear, so they cry, and I will not hear, saith the LORD of hosts: 14 and I will scatter them with a whirlwind among all the nations whom they knew not. Thus the land was desolate after them, that no man passed through nor returned: for they laid the pleasant land desolate.

7.3.1.en: The Lord assures them that His speaking about fasting after the period of seventy years of humiliation is the very speaking He addressed to them by the prophets before the captivity; He does not ask for fasts, or for eating and drinking (the feasts), as an end in themselves... “Is not this the word which the LORD hath cried by the former prophets, when Jerusalem was inhabited and at rest, and the cities thereof round about her, and the south and the plain inhabited?” [7]. The word of the Lord does not change in a time of distress or a time of prosperity, for He asks for the holy life, and then He accepts their fasts as well as their feasts and smells in their worship a savor of delight. Thus God does not separate spiritual conduct from spiritual worship, therefore He asks of them the following:

7.4.0.en: First: “Execute true judgment” [9]. If we offer fasting that we may enjoy God's mercies, it does not befit us to judge our brethren unjustly, lest we hear the words of the Lord: “How long will ye judge unjustly, and accept the persons of the wicked? Judge the lowly and the fatherless; do justice to the poor and needy” (Ps 82:2-3). Habakkuk cried to the Lord, saying: “Before me are plundering and injustice, and strife ariseth and contention lifteth itself up. Therefore the law is slacked, and judgment doth never go forth: for the wicked doth compass about the righteous; therefore judgment goeth forth crooked” (Hab 1:3-4).

7.4.1.en: He began with judging truly, that is, He directed the speech to the spiritual leaders, since it befits them, before they decide on the fast or cease from it, or celebrate the joyful feast, that they review their accounts in their practical life, whether they practice justice so that God hears them and accepts their counsel, or practice injustice so that they benefit neither from fasting nor from feasts! Would that they hold fast to justice and truth, listening to the words of St. Jerome on the tongue of the Lord: [I gave you authority over My flock and over the people of God, so be judges and not wolves].

7.4.2.en: Second: “Do kindness and mercy, every man with his brother, and oppress not the widow, nor the fatherless, nor the stranger, nor the poor” [9-10]. Along with commitment to justice and truth, every man is also committed to kindness and mercy with his brother. It befits us to bear the spirit of our Lord Jesus crucified, where on the Cross He proclaimed the embrace of justice and mercy together. He fulfilled the divine debt on our behalf, declaring His justice and His mercy without contradiction. So that God may smell our worship with its fasts and feasts, it befits us to walk in the spirit of truth without carelessness, and in the spirit of love and mercy without harshness or tyranny.

7.4.3.en: St. Jerome offers us an example of good conduct, saying: [Indeed, the wicked man plays many roles like one acting on a stage: when he is hungry he puts on the mask of a lion to devour, and when he seizes the possessions of others he puts on the mask of a wolf, and when he kills he puts on the mask of a killer, etc... So, with the difference, it befits the saints to have different masks, but good ones. When I give alms I am like one who puts on the mask of the tender man, and when I judge with truth I put on the mask of the good judge, and when I bear injury with humility I wear the mask of the humble... Wretched is the man who has the masks of evil, and happy is he who has varied goodness. With the same thought I say that in life we live like those who play many short roles: I put on our Lord Jesus Christ within me, so that He is the mask of truth when I judge, and the mask of sincere fatherhood when I meet the orphans, and the mask of tender love when I deal with the poor, etc...

7.4.4.en: If we wish to practice a fast acceptable to God or to celebrate a feast joyful to Him, let us care for all our brethren, especially the widow, the fatherless, the stranger and the poor, bearing love without hatred in the heart even toward our brethren who trouble us.

7.4.5.en: St. Didymus the Blind offers us spiritual concepts of the widow, the fatherless, the stranger and the poor, for the praiseworthy widow is she who has lost her wicked husband, who is Satan, to seek her true Bridegroom our Lord Jesus, and the good fatherless is he who has lost his father who begot him in sin as he hears the voice: “Forget also thine own people, and thy father's house” (Ps 45:10), so that the Lord Himself may be a father to him leading him to the heights. For it was said of God: “he relieveth the fatherless and widow” (Ps 146:9), “A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows” (Ps 68:5). He also cares for the stranger who left “idol worship,” his old homeland, to set out toward the Jerusalem above, as He cares for the poor who left everything and counted it as refuse that he might win Christ.

7.4.6.en: Thus may we set out with this holy company, the souls that were widowed to win the heavenly Bridegroom, and became fatherless to receive God as their Father, and became strangers to set out to the heavenly things, and became poor to acquire the pearl of great price!

7.5.0.en: Third: “and let none of you imagine evil against his brother in your heart” [10]. St. Didymus the Blind says: [After this teaching concerning not wronging those deprived of care and protection, Scripture strongly affirms that it befits us to forget insults, not by words only but from the depth of the heart... In the same sense we recall the saying of the Savior in the Gospel: “For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you” (Mt 6:14)].

7.5.1.en: The Lord Christ gave us the parable of the servant who owed ten thousand talents (Mt 18:23-35); since his lord forgave him his debt, it befitted him to pardon his brother, but since he did not pardon him he lost the grace of his lord. The Lord commented on the parable, saying: “So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses” (Mt 18:35).

7.6.0.en: Fourth: Obedience to the commandment and hearing the voice of the Lord, for He says: “But they refused to hearken, and gave a stubborn shoulder, and made heavy their ears, that they should not hear. Yea, they made their heart an adamant stone, lest they should hear the law, and the words which the LORD of hosts hath sent in his spirit by the former prophets: therefore came a great wrath from the LORD of hosts” [11-12]. This is the summary of all their evil: “hardness of the inner heart,” which closes the door of God's mercies in their face so that they fall under His wrath.

7.6.1.en: Concerning hearing the Law or the commandment, St. Didymus the Blind says: [The Lord who gave them the Law commanded them this worship: “Give ear, O my people, to my law” (Ps 77:1), and that they follow this call: “in his law doth he meditate day and night” (Ps 1:2)... “And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart: and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up. And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thine hand, and they shall be as frontlets between thine eyes. And thou shalt write them upon the posts of thy house, and on thy gates” (Deut 6:6-8). By our obedience to the commandments given to us we are counted faithful and hearers of the Law. How could he not truly be faithful and a hearer so long as he keeps the holy words in his soul and heart and speaks of them in his house as in the way, in his sleep as in his waking?! For in his sleep he says to the One who knows all things: “When I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches” (Ps 63:6). And in his waking he utters the same thing, remembering in his thought the words of our Lord, saying boldly: “O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee” (Ps 63:1). And with the same longing he says with the prophet Isaiah: “With my soul have I desired thee in the night” (Isa 26:9)].

7.6.2.en: He who does not hear the Law has “a stubborn shoulder,” that is, he turns his back to the Law in stubbornness, and as St. Didymus says: [This happens when we are rooted in evil, so we deserve the rebukes of Psalm 49: “But unto the wicked God saith, What hast thou to do to declare my statutes, or that thou shouldest take my covenant in thy mouth? Seeing thou hatest instruction, and castest my words behind thee” (Ps 49:16-17)... He who turns his back to the words of the Lord ignores them without feeling, so that he turns his back on the giver of these words. They are mad and full of folly, for they insult the Lord who laid down the Law by transgressing His Law, and as the Apostle says: “Thou that makest thy boast of the law, through breaking the law dishonourest thou God?” (Rom 2:23)... They turn their backs to Him who speaks to them: “they have turned unto me the back, and not the face” (Jer 2:27), though it should have been on the contrary that they present the face to the Creator of all things... [Unto thee lift I up mine eyes, O thou that dwellest in the heavens] (Ps 123:1), and also: “Mine eyes are ever toward the LORD; for he shall pluck my feet out of the net” (Ps 25:15)].

7.6.3.en: He who does not hear the Law has also ears heavy of hearing, and as St. Didymus says: [The stubborn shoulder is the fruit of the ear heavy of hearing, and not the ear of the body but the ear of the soul. It was said: “The wicked are estranged from the womb: they go astray as soon as they be born, speaking lies. Their poison is like the poison of a serpent: they are like the deaf adder that stoppeth her ear; which will not hearken to the voice of charmers, charming never so wisely” (Ps 58:4-6). “How could he not be stubborn and deaf who makes his ear heavy and stops it, who from his birth is a stranger to the Lord, speaking lies while in the womb?! This can also apply in a symbolic way to those who became strangers from their birth to the Church their mother, withdrew from her, preferring falsehoods from their coming out of the womb, and stopped their ears like the serpent, so their energy became the work of evil and the spreading of poison].

7.6.4.en: St. Didymus also sees that the prophet Isaiah bears witness concerning these ears of the soul that are heavy of hearing, saying: “Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and convert, and be healed” (Isa 6:10). “For since they delight in the whirlpool of evil and unbelief which they chose for themselves, their ears became heavy and their eyes were shut and their heart became fat, so they do not hear the talk about virtue and the knowledge of the truth that is able to make them virtuous and return them to the One from whom they departed, He who is able to heal them from blindness and deafness...”].

7.6.5.en: It is to be noted in the discourse before us the affirmation of human freedom, for with their full will they refused to hear, and made their ears heavy, etc... a matter which Holy Scripture affirms in both its Testaments.

7.7.0.en: Fifth: God repays their not hearing Him with His not hearing them, for He says: “Therefore came a great wrath from the LORD of hosts. And as he cried, and they would not hear, so they cry, and I will not hear, saith the LORD of hosts, and I will scatter them with a whirlwind among all the nations whom they knew not. Thus the land was desolate after them, that no man passed through nor returned: for they laid the pleasant land desolate” [12-14].

7.7.1.en: God in His love threatens with wrath so that when we cry to Him: “Be not wroth very sore, O LORD” (Isa 64:8), “Wilt thou be angry with us for ever? wilt thou draw out thine anger to all generations?” (Ps 85:6), we find grace in His eyes. For the Lord in His wrath, as St. Didymus the Blind says, does not avenge Himself but punishes to make us virtuous, putting an end to sin as a disease that has afflicted us or wounds in us, for He “will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth” (2 Tim 2:4). By His wrath He reveals His care for our salvation, therefore it was said: “When my wrath cometh, I will heal him again” (Isa 7:4), as says one who was healed of his wounds: “O LORD, I will praise thee: though thou wast angry with me, thine anger is turned away, and thou comfortedst me” (Isa 12:1). St. Didymus the Blind says: [The wrath of our Lord, since a harvest of good comes with it, is not evil but is necessary. It is the work of the Physician of souls who is “healing all manner of sickness and all manner of disease among the people” (Mt 4:23)... As a wise physician, a maker of good things, He uses a painful and hateful treatment, as the prophet bears witness... “Yet he also is wise, and will bring evil, and will not call back his words” (Isa 31:2)].

7.8.0.en: He disciplines them, declaring: “I will scatter them with a whirlwind among all the nations whom they knew not” [14], though He did not scatter them at that time in all the world but permitted their captivity by Assyria and Babylon, two nations known to them at that time, which shows that the threat carried a clear prophecy of what would happen to them through their rejection of the Lord Christ and their disobedience to Him, so that they would be scattered in the whole world, among nations which they had not yet known.

7.8.1.en: What are these nations under whose captivity man falls by his rejection of faith in God but the varied evils, as the Scripture says: “Wherefore God also gave them up to uncleanness through the lusts of their own hearts” (Rom 1:24), “God gave them over to a reprobate mind, because they did not like to retain God in their knowledge” (Rom 1:28). For by men's rejection of the knowledge of God the grace of God abandons them and they fall under the captivity of sins and it is said of them: “being filled with all unrighteousness” (Rom 1:29); these are the nations foreign to the nature of man whom God created in His image! Because of stubbornness the land is laid waste and its delight turns to desolation, and there is neither going nor returning in it; thus by sin the body (the land) is corrupted and the life of man turns into a life of gloom and barrenness, losing inner peace, joy of heart and spiritual fruit.
